findings.claim: The try/except in _build_snapshot guarding the signing-keys read catches only RuntimeError. subprocess.TimeoutExpired (and FileNotFoundError if git is absent) are not subclasses of RuntimeError; they are subclasses of OSError. A 30-second git timeout reading docs/security/mcp-signing-keys.pub raises subprocess.TimeoutExpired, which escapes the except clause at line 581, leaves signing_keys_body unbound, and propagates uncaught out of _build_snapshot() through snapshot() to every resource-read caller. The server transitions from the intended 'degrade gracefully with null key-id' mode to 'fail all resource reads with an uncaught exception' mode — the inverse of the designed safety posture.
findings.evidence: resources.py:564–583: try block calls _read_committed_text (line 565) → _git_stdout (line 104) → subprocess.run(..., timeout=_RESOURCE_GIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS) (line 113). subprocess.run raises subprocess.TimeoutExpired on timeout; TimeoutExpired inherits from subprocess.SubprocessError → OSError → Exception, not from RuntimeError. The except clause at line 581 is 'except RuntimeError as error:' — TimeoutExpired is not caught. signing_keys_body at line 566 is assigned only inside the try block or in the except block; on TimeoutExpired escape it is unbound and NameError follows immediately at line 585 in the caller. Neither outage regression test injects a TimeoutExpired — both inject RuntimeError paths only (malformed parse → RuntimeError from _parse_signing_keys; empty keyring → RuntimeError raised explicitly in _build_snapshot).
findings.impact: On a host under I/O pressure or with a slow git object store, git show for mcp-signing-keys.pub can exceed _RESOURCE_GIT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (30 s). Every subsequent call to catalog.snapshot() — invoked by read_static, read_rule, read_waiver, read_finding, read_decision — re-enters _build_snapshot (because self._snapshot is not updated on failure), re-times out, and raises again. The MCP resource layer is fully dark rather than serving degraded responses with null key-id. Duration equals wall-clock time until server restart or git recovery.
findings.mitigation: Widen the except clause at resources.py:581 to 'except (RuntimeError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired, OSError) as error:'. The TimeoutExpired message is human-readable ('Command … timed out after 30 seconds') and propagates cleanly through str(error) into _degraded_signing_keys_payload. Add a regression test that patches _git_stdout to raise subprocess.TimeoutExpired and asserts: snapshot().key_id is None, signing-keys error field contains the timeout message, caplog contains 'degrading MCP resource snapshot', and all other static resources remain accessible with key_id=None.

findings.claim: subscribe(), unsubscribe(), and _schedule_resource_update_notifications() access self._subscribers without holding any lock, while snapshot() modifies self._snapshot under self._snapshot_lock. In the HTTP transport (021H) with concurrent connections, concurrent subscribe/unsubscribe calls from separate threads race against notification dispatch, exposing a check-then-act hazard in unsubscribe() and a set-growth race in subscribe().
findings.evidence: resources.py:480–488: subscribe() calls self._subscribers.setdefault(uri, set()).add(session) — two operations, not atomic. unsubscribe() at lines 483–488 reads subscribers = self._subscribers.get(uri) then conditionally calls subscribers.discard() and self._subscribers.pop(uri) — three operations, not atomic. _schedule_resource_update_notifications() at lines 552–558 takes list() snapshots of .items() and sessions, which mitigates mid-iteration mutation but does not prevent a concurrent unsubscribe() from removing the set between the list() call and the loop body, or a concurrent subscribe() from adding a session that receives a duplicate notification. _snapshot_lock (line 453) guards only snapshot state.
findings.impact: In the current stdio transport the asyncio event loop serialises session callbacks so the race window is negligible. In the 021H HTTP transport with concurrent connections, a subscribe/unsubscribe race could cause: (a) a missed resource-update notification to a subscribing session, or (b) an AttributeError if unsubscribe() pops the set while _schedule_resource_update_notifications is mid-iteration. Frequency is low; user-visible effect is a stale cache at the MCP client that re-polls on the next commit anyway.
findings.mitigation: Add a self._subscribers_lock = threading.Lock() alongside self._snapshot_lock. Acquire it in subscribe(), unsubscribe(), and around the iteration block in _schedule_resource_update_notifications(). The lock need not be held during the async loop.create_task() calls — only during dict read/write.
